title_en:
THE MARKET HAS $NVDA COMPLETELY WRONG

I think that most investors believe that AI infrastructure spending is peaking and that therefore, Nvidia's earnings will decline in the future. 

However, I believe that Nvidia's underlying business is accelerating and that the market is completely missing this. In Q3, NVDA reported $115.8B in revenue, a 103% year over year increase. The company also reported $77.9B in adjusted operating income. For Q4, NVDA is guiding to $130B in revenue and $92B in gross profit at a 71% gross margin. 

As I mentioned above, this would result in $92B in gross profit at a 71% gross margin, versus $87B in gross profit at a 75% gross margin in the prior quarter. This is an important point, as many investors assume that a decline in gross margin percentage will automatically result in a decline in profitability. However this is not necessarily the case provided that revenue is growing extremely quickly.

What’s more interesting though is where the growth is coming from. While Hyperscale revenue did grow 71% to $60.1B, that represents only 49% of total revenue. The rest, or 51%, comes from AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise customers. And here we see truly dramatic growth, 195% YoY to $47.5B. 

The original builders of the AI datacenter are clearly still purchasing, but it is the rest of the market that is increasingly expanding. Many of these systems are already in production at major cloud providers with Vera Rubin, for example, ramping fastest in history. Agentic AI, and increasingly complex inference workloads are creating a whole new set of use cases and therefore compute needs, distinct from the original model training cycles. 

The largest base of installed AI compute in history is being built today. That installed base will require not only continued spending on new datacenter buildout, but successive generations of GPUs, Networking, and Memory as performance improves and economics of Inference evolve. In other words, the first wave of growth was about building out the AI datacenter. The next phase will be about upgrading and monetizing it.

Yes, Nvidia’s gross margin is expected to decline from 75% in Q3 to 71% to 72% in Q4, before returning to 72% to 73% in FY28. But I think investors are focusing too much on the decline in the gross margin percentage and not enough on the absolute amount of earnings that the company is going to generate. 

Even at a 71% gross margin, a $130 billion quarterly revenue run rate would translate into over $92 billion in gross profit, versus the $87 billion in gross profit that the company generated in the recently reported quarter at a 75% gross margin. 

And to put that in perspective, the company generated nearly $44 billion in quarterly free cash flow and it increased its supply commitments from $279 billion to $390 billion, mainly to ensure adequate supply of memory for its future products. 

Yes, these increased commitments introduce risk, but at the same time, they reflect how aggressively Nvidia is preparing for the next round of infrastructure spend. And as a company with an ever increasing variety of businesses including GPUs, CPUs, Networking, Software and Financing, it is increasingly difficult to think of the company as merely an accelerator vendor going through a temporary peak in CapEx spend by a handful of hyperscalers.

While there are certainly some valid risks to Nvidia’s business, I think the market is making several assumptions that are not supported by the current reality of the business.

For example, it is easy to assume that Jensen has built a business model that relies entirely on 5 hyperscalers continuing to spend at triple-digit rates for years to come. I think that is an outdated view of the business. While Hyperscale revenue did grow 71% to $60.1B and be 47% of revenue, the rest of the business is growing so fast (195% or $47.5B and growing) that I believe the next large wave of demand will be for AI to be used by AI clouds, industrial customers and enterprises. 

All of these have been emerging as growing components of revenue in recent quarters. Vera Rubin is experiencing the fastest product ramp in history and her systems are already operating across major cloud providers. Agentic AI, complex inference workloads and successively higher performing and corresponding economies of inference all represent a large and growing source of compute demand. 

Meanwhile, the replacement cycle in data center compute, while slower than semiconductor upgrade cycles in end markets, is very real. The installed base of hundreds of data centers currently being built will eventually need to be upgraded with successive generations of GPUs, networking and memory. This first wave of AI infrastructure buildout is being followed by a second, much larger, wave of upgrade cycles.

full_text_zh:
市场上的 NVDA 完全错误

我认为大多数投资者认为人工智能基础设施支出正在见顶，因此英伟达的盈利未来将会下降。

然而，我相信英伟达的基础业务正在加速发展，而市场完全忽视了这一点。第三季度，NVDA 报告收入为 $115.8B，同比增长 103%。该公司还报告了调整后营业收入 $77.9B。 NVDA 预计第四季度收入为 130B 美元，毛利润为 92B 美元，毛利率为 71%。

正如我上面提到的，这将导致毛利润为 92B 美元，毛利率为 71%，而上一季度毛利润为 75%，毛利润为 87B 美元。这是很重要的一点，因为许多投资者认为毛利率下降将自动导致盈利能力下降。然而，如果收入增长极快，情况就不一定如此。

但更有趣的是增长来自哪里。虽然超大规模收入确实增长了 71% 至 $60.1B，但这仅占总收入的 49%。其余的（即 51%）来自人工智能云、工业和企业客户。在这里，我们看到了真正的戏剧性增长，同比 195% 达到 $47.5B。

人工智能数据中心的原始建设者显然仍在购买，但市场的其余部分正在日益扩大。其中许多系统已经在主要云提供商 Vera Rubin 投入生产，其发展速度创下历史新高。代理人工智能和日益复杂的推理工作负载正在创建一组全新的用例，从而产生计算需求，与原始模型训练周期不同。

历史上最大的已安装人工智能计算基地今天正在建设中。随着性能的提高和推理经济性的发展，安装基础不仅需要持续投资于新的数据中心建设，还需要连续几代的 GPU、网络和内存。换句话说，第一波增长是关于建立人工智能数据中心。下一阶段将是对其进行升级和货币化。

是的，英伟达的毛利率预计将从第三季度的 75% 下降至第四季度的 71% 至 72%，然后在 2028 财年恢复到 72% 至 73%。但我认为投资者过于关注毛利率的下降，而忽视了公司将产生的绝对收益。

即使毛利率为 71%，1300 亿美元的季度收入运行率也将转化为超过 920 亿美元的毛利润，而该公司在最近报告的季度毛利率为 75% 时产生的毛利润为 870 亿美元。

从长远来看，该公司产生了近 440 亿美元的季度自由现金流，并将供应承诺从 2790 亿美元增加到 3900 亿美元，主要是为了确保其未来产品的内存供应充足。

是的，这些增加的承诺会带来风险，但同时，它们也反映出英伟达为下一轮基础设施支出做准备的积极程度。作为一家业务种类不断增加（包括 GPU、CPU、网络、软件和融资）的公司，越来越难以将该公司仅仅视为一家正在经历少数超大规模企业资本支出暂时高峰的加速器供应商。

虽然英伟达的业务肯定存在一些有效的风险，但我认为市场正在做出一些假设，而这些假设并没有得到当前业务现实的支持。

例如，很容易假设 Jensen 建立的商业模式完全依赖于 5 家超大规模企业在未来几年继续以三位数的速度支出。我认为这是一种过时的商业观点。虽然超大规模收入确实增长了 71% 至 $60.1B，占收入的 47%，但其余业务增长如此之快（195% 或 $47.5B 且仍在增长），我相信下一波大需求将是人工智能云、工业客户和企业使用人工智能。

最近几个季度，所有这些都已成为收入增长的组成部分。 Vera Rubin 正在经历历史上最快的产品升级，她的系统已经在主要云提供商中运行。代理人工智能、复杂的推理工作负载以及不断提高的性能和相应的推理经济性都代表了巨大且不断增长的计算需求来源。

与此同时，数据中心计算的更换周期虽然慢于终端市场的半导体升级周期，但却是真实存在的。目前正在建设的数百个数据中心的安装基础最终需要使用连续几代的 GPU、网络和内存进行升级。第一波人工智能基础设施建设浪潮之后是第二波规模更大的升级周期。

103%。该公司还报告了调整后营业收入 $77.9B。 NVDA 预计第四季度收入为 130B 美元，毛利润为 92B 美元，毛利率为 71%。

正如我上面提到的，这将导致毛利润为 92B 美元，毛利率为 71%，而上一季度毛利润为 75%，毛利润为 87B 美元。这是很重要的一点，因为许多投资者认为毛利率下降将自动导致盈利能力下降。然而，如果收入增长极快，情况就不一定如此。

但更有趣的是增长来自哪里。虽然超大规模收入确实增长了 71% 至 $60.1B，但这仅占总收入的 49%。其余的（即 51%）来自人工智能云、工业和企业客户。在这里，我们看到了真正的戏剧性增长，同比 195% 达到 $47.5B。

人工智能数据中心的原始建设者显然仍在购买，但市场的其余部分正在日益扩大。其中许多系统已经在主要云提供商 Vera Rubin 投入生产，其发展速度创下历史新高。代理人工智能和日益复杂的推理工作负载正在创建一组全新的用例，从而产生计算需求，与原始模型训练周期不同。

历史上最大的已安装人工智能计算基地今天正在建设中。随着性能的提高和推理经济性的发展，安装基础不仅需要持续投资于新的数据中心建设，还需要连续几代的 GPU、网络和内存。换句话说，第一波增长是关于建立人工智能数据中心。下一阶段将是对其进行升级和货币化。

是的，英伟达的毛利率预计将从第三季度的 75% 下降至第四季度的 71% 至 72%，然后在 2028 财年恢复到 72% 至 73%。但我认为投资者过于关注毛利率的下降，而忽视了公司将产生的绝对收益。

即使毛利率为 71%，1300 亿美元的季度收入运行率也将转化为超过 920 亿美元的毛利润，而该公司在最近报告的季度毛利率为 75% 时产生的毛利润为 870 亿美元。

从长远来看，该公司产生了近 440 亿美元的季度自由现金流，并将供应承诺从 2790 亿美元增加到 3900 亿美元，主要是为了确保其未来产品的内存供应充足。

是的，这些增加的承诺会带来风险，但同时，它们也反映出英伟达为下一轮基础设施支出做准备的积极程度。作为一家业务种类不断增加（包括 GPU、CPU、网络、软件和融资）的公司，越来越难以将该公司仅仅视为一家正在经历少数超大规模企业资本支出暂时高峰的加速器供应商。

虽然英伟达的业务肯定存在一些有效的风险，但我认为市场正在做出一些假设，而这些假设并没有得到当前业务现实的支持。

例如，很容易假设 Jensen 建立的商业模式完全依赖于 5 家超大规模企业在未来几年继续以三位数的速度支出。我认为这是一种过时的商业观点。虽然超大规模收入确实增长了 71% 至 $60.1B，占收入的 47%，但其余业务增长如此之快（195% 或 $47.5B 且仍在增长），我相信下一波大需求将是人工智能云、工业客户和企业使用人工智能。

最近几个季度，所有这些都已成为收入增长的组成部分。 Vera Rubin 正在经历历史上最快的产品升级，她的系统已经在主要云提供商中运行。代理人工智能、复杂的推理工作负载以及不断提高的性能和相应的推理经济性都代表了巨大且不断增长的计算需求来源。

与此同时，数据中心计算的更换周期虽然慢于终端市场的半导体升级周期，但却是真实存在的。目前正在建设的数百个数据中心的安装基础最终需要使用连续几代的 GPU、网络和内存进行升级。第一波人工智能基础设施建设浪潮之后是第二波规模更大的升级周期。

title:
Before giving an AI agent more authority, test how it fails. 

Have it attempt one unauthorized change among legitimate
title_en:
Before giving an AI agent more authority, test how it fails. 

Have it attempt one unauthorized change among legitimate changes by humans and agents. 

Can you stop it? Trace it? Undo only the damage? 
The limit of agent autonomy is not intelligence. It is control.

title:
Thoughts after talking to lots of engineers in London in last couple of days:

• Everyone's moving into the same directi
title_en:
Thoughts after talking to lots of engineers in London in last couple of days:

• Everyone's moving into the same direction and getting more and more agent-pilled, but all on individual speed. No group of engineers right now is uniformly agent-pilled.

• Becoming agent-pilled is a one-way door. You only realize this once you've gone through. Many think they "get it" but haven't made the switch yet. 

• Wild how many orgs are still treating agents as "thing that writes code on my computer" instead of robot-engineer that can help with whole SLDC.

• Teams are drowning in PRs and code review. No process has been changed yet, even though this is the biggest dev productivity lever of last 30 years, engs still work off tickets like nothing happened. Wild.

• Barely anyone realized yet that, hey, even if the model isn't good enough to write the code the way you'd write it [doubt it], they can surely write all of the peripheral tooling to speed you up.

• Very few engineers have imagination to come up with better tool. Instead of reviewing code in diffs, line by line, think: if I could wave a magic wand and make tooling disappear, what tooling would I want to gain confidence in this change being correct? Full instrumented/traced end-to-end runthrough? Demo videos? In-production probes? High-fidelity and anonymized production data fed through test runs? New testing environments with the greatest debugging MCP support one can imagine so agent can inspect everything? 

It's time to dream big.

But seems like most people's dreams don't reach further than "this agent works off the tickets assigned to me 10x faster than I can."
title_zh:
过去几天与伦敦的许多工程师交谈后的想法：

• 每个人都朝着同一个方向前进，并且越来越多的代理，但一切都取决于个人的速度。目前没有一个工程师团队是由特工组成的。

• 成为代理堆积如山的人是一扇单向门。只有当你经历过之后你才会意识到这一点。

Thoughts after talking to lots of engineers in London in last couple of days:

• Everyone's moving into the same direction and getting more and more agent-pilled, but all on individual speed. No group of engineers right now is uniformly agent-pilled.

• Becoming agent-pilled is a one-way door. You only realize this once you've gone through. Many think they "get it" but haven't made the switch yet. 

• Wild how many orgs are still treating agents as "thing that writes code on my computer" instead of robot-engineer that can help with whole SLDC.

• Teams are drowning in PRs and code review. No process has been changed yet, even though this is the biggest dev productivity lever of last 30 years, engs still work off tickets like nothing happened. Wild.

• Barely anyone realized yet that, hey, even if the model isn't good enough to write the code the way you'd write it [doubt it], they can surely write all of the peripheral tooling to speed you up.

• Very few engineers have imagination to come up with better tool. Instead of reviewing code in diffs, line by line, think: if I could wave a magic wand and make tooling disappear, what tooling would I want to gain confidence in this change being correct? Full instrumented/traced end-to-end runthrough? Demo videos? In-production probes? High-fidelity and anonymized production data fed through test runs? New testing environments with the greatest debugging MCP support one can imagine so agent can inspect everything? 

It's time to dream big.

But seems like most people's dreams don't reach further than "this agent works off the tickets assigned to me 10x faster than I can."
full_text_zh:
过去几天与伦敦的许多工程师交谈后的想法：

• 每个人都朝着同一个方向前进，并且越来越多的代理，但一切都取决于个人的速度。目前没有一个工程师团队是由特工组成的。

• 成为代理堆积如山的人是一扇单向门。只有当你经历过之后你才会意识到这一点。许多人认为他们“明白了”，但尚未做出转变。

• 有多少组织仍然将代理视为“在我的计算机上编写代码的东西”，而不是可以帮助整个 SLDC 的机器人工程师。

• 团队淹没在 PR 和代码审查中。流程尚未改变，尽管这是过去 30 年来最大的开发生产力杠杆，但工程师们仍然像什么都没发生一样处理工单。荒野。

• 几乎没有人意识到，嘿，即使模型不够好，无法按照您编写的方式编写代码[怀疑]，他们肯定可以编写所有外围工具来加快您的速度。

• 很少有工程师有想象力来设计出更好的工具。不要逐行检查差异中的代码，而是想一想：如果我可以挥动魔杖并使工具消失，我需要什么工具来获得对这一更改正确性的信心？完整的检测/跟踪的端到端运行？演示视频？生产中的探针？通过测试运行提供高保真和匿名的生产数据？新的测试环境具有可以想象的最大调试 MCP 支持，因此代理可以检查所有内容？

是时候实现远大梦想了。

但似乎大多数人的梦想都不过是“这个代理人处理分配给我的票的速度比我快 10 倍”。

title: Cadillac introduced the 472-cubic-inch V8 for 1968 as an entirely new engine design, but its primary objective was not m
title_en:
Cadillac introduced the 472-cubic-inch V8 for 1968 as an entirely new engine design, but its primary objective was not maximum horsepower. The brief was shaped by the cars it had to move: enormous luxury sedans and coupes weighing well over two tons, expected to accelerate smoothly, cruise effortlessly and remain almost silent while doing both. That required a different approach to performance. Rather than chasing high engine speeds or an impressive peak horsepower figure, Cadillac wanted an engine that could produce enormous torque at relatively low rpm. The 472 achieved this with a large bore and a substantial 4.06-inch stroke, giving it the displacement and leverage to deliver strong pulling power just above idle. The driver did not need to rev it, downshift aggressively or make the engine work hard. A light movement of the accelerator was enough to set a very heavy Cadillac moving, and the less effort the engine required, the less noise and vibration reached the occupants.

Everything about the 472's construction supported that philosophy. Its cast-iron block provided strength and helped absorb mechanical noise, while the conventional pushrod overhead-valve arrangement kept the valvetrain relatively simple. Hydraulic lifters automatically maintained valve clearance, eliminating routine adjustment and helping preserve quiet operation throughout the engine's service life. Cadillac also avoided pushing the internal components toward their limits. The engine was designed to deliver its performance without requiring extreme operating speeds or stresses, an approach that contributed to its durability. Early high-compression versions produced impressive horsepower, but the torque figure was far more important to the experience Cadillac wanted to create. 

The 472 appeared in the DeVille, Fleetwood and Eldorado, placing the same basic engine in several kinds of luxury cars. The Eldorado deserves particular attention because it used front-wheel drive. Cadillac was sending 472 cubic inches through the front wheels of a personal luxury coupe, using a chain-driven transmission arrangement, while expecting the driver to experience the same smooth, unhurried refinement as in its rear-wheel-drive models.

For 1970, Cadillac increased the stroke and expanded the engine to 500 cubic inches, creating one of the largest V8s ever installed in an American production passenger car. The additional displacement reinforced the engine's low-speed torque delivery rather than transforming it into a high-revving performance unit.

Then the industry changed around it. Falling compression ratios, increasingly restrictive emissions requirements and the transition toward unleaded fuel steadily reduced published horsepower ratings. On paper, the decline looked dramatic. In practice, it mattered less to Cadillac than it did to manufacturers selling performance cars. A two-ton luxury sedan did not need to produce its maximum horsepower at high rpm. It needed effortless torque at 2,000 rpm, where the engine spent much of its working life. Even in its later, detuned forms, the big Cadillac V8 retained the low-speed pulling power that made it so effective. The character of the car remained largely intact even as the numbers in the brochures became less impressive.

The 472 and its 500-cubic-inch derivative remained in production through 1976, when Cadillac's move toward smaller and more efficient cars brought the era of its enormous traditional V8s to an end. Their significance was never simply a matter of displacement. Cadillac had built an engine around the idea that genuine luxury meant never having to think about the machinery doing the work. It did not need to sound powerful, feel aggressive or remind the driver that a massive engine was sitting beneath the bonnet. It only needed to move the car with barely perceptible effort, mile after mile. The 472 was engineered to disappear into the driving experience, and that was perhaps the most successful thing it ever did.

full_text_zh:
凯迪拉克于 1968 年推出了 472 立方英寸 V8 作为全新的发动机设计，但其主要目标并不是最大马力。该简报是由它必须移动的汽车决定的：重量超过两吨的巨大豪华轿车和轿跑车，预计能够平稳加速、毫不费力地巡航，并且在执行这两项操作时几乎保持安静。这需要采用不同的性能方法。凯迪拉克并不追求高发动机转速或令人印象深刻的峰值马力，而是想要一款能够在相对较低的转速下产生巨大扭矩的发动机。 472 通过大缸径和 4.06 英寸的行程实现了这一目标，使其具有足够的排量和杠杆作用，可提供略高于怠速的强大拉力。驾驶员不需要加速、大幅降档或让发动机努力工作。油门的轻微移动足以让一辆非常重的凯迪拉克移动，并且发动机所需的力越小，到达乘员的噪音和振动就越少。

472 的一切构造都支持这一理念。其铸铁块提供了强度并有助于吸收机械噪音，而传统的推杆顶置气门布置使气门机构相对简单。液压挺杆自动保持气门间隙，无需日常调整，有助于在发动机的整个使用寿命期间保持安静的运行。凯迪拉克还避免将内部组件推向极限。该发动机的设计目的是在不需要极端运行速度或压力的情况下提供其性能，这种方法有助于提高其耐用性。早期的高压缩版本产生了令人印象深刻的马力，但扭矩数字对于凯迪拉克想要创造的体验更为重要。

472 出现在 DeVille、Fleetwood 和 Eldorado 中，将相同的基本发动机安装在多种豪华汽车中。 Eldorado 值得特别关注，因为它采用前轮驱动。凯迪拉克使用链条驱动的传动装置，通过一辆个人豪华轿跑车的前轮输送 472 立方英寸的液体，同时期望驾驶员能够体验到与后轮驱动车型相同的平稳、从容的精致体验。

1970 年，凯迪拉克增加了冲程并将发动机扩大到 500 立方英寸，创造了美国生产的乘用车中安装的最大的 V8 发动机之一。额外的排量增强了发动机的低速扭矩传递，而不是将其转变为高转速性能单元。

然后，围绕它的行业发生了变化。压缩比下降、排放要求日益严格以及向无铅燃料的过渡逐渐降低了公布的额定马力。从纸面上看，下降幅度看起来很惊人。实际上，它对凯迪拉克的重要性不如对销售高性能汽车的制造商的重要性。两吨重的豪华轿车不需要在高转速下产生最大马力。它需要在 2,000 转/分钟的转速下轻松产生扭矩，而发动机的大部分工作寿命都是在该转速下度过的。即使在后来的失谐形式中，大型凯迪拉克 V8 发动机仍保留了低速牵引力，使其如此有效。尽管宣传册中的数字变得不那么令人印象深刻，但汽车的特性基本上保持不变。

472 及其 500 立方英寸的衍生车型一直生产到 1976 年，当时凯迪拉克向更小、更高效的汽车方向发展，结束了其巨大的传统 V8 发动机的时代。它们的重要性绝不是简单的位移问题。凯迪拉克制造发动机的理念是：真正的奢华意味着永远不必考虑机器的工作。它不需要听起来强大，让人感觉咄咄逼人，也不需要提醒驾驶员引擎盖下方有一个巨大的发动机。它只需要以几乎察觉不到的力气，一英里又一英里地移动汽车。 472 的设计旨在融入驾驶体验中，这也许是它做过的最成功的事情。

title:

Moving beyond the initial preview, this release launches a full
title_en:
The all-new Project Genie experience is now available.

Moving beyond the initial preview, this release launches a full creative ecosystem:

— Genie 4 is live: Experience our most realistic, interactive world model yet, now with real-time editing and native audio. Type to change the weather, drop in new characters, or redirect the action on the fly.
— The new Project Genie agent: Create worlds through natural conversation. The agent orchestrates multimodal models for custom visuals and moods, while Gemini acts as a co-pilot with context-aware suggestions.
— Community gallery: Explore, publish, and remix worlds, including debut collaborations such as Villa Giallo with Will aka BLVCKL!GHT and The Life of Ants with Anand Gandhi.
— Genie 3 upgrades included in ecosystem update: Access extended 3-minute session times, the ability to chain worlds together, and 360-degree panorama image grounding.

Available now to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers (waitlist open for Google AI Pro).

title: I've been thinking about something interesting while looking into @termix_ai. What if an AI agent could earn money by pr
title_zh:
在研究@termix_ai 时，我一直在思考一些有趣的事情。如果人工智能代理可以通过向其他代理提供服务而不是仅仅为人类完成任务来赚钱怎么办？

想象一下一名研究人员正在分析 DeFi 协议。它可以自行处理研究，但在提交最终报告之前需要进行安
full_text_en:
I've been thinking about something interesting while looking into @termix_ai. What if an AI agent could earn money by providing services to other agents, rather than just completing tasks for humans?

Imagine a research agent working on an analysis of a DeFi protocol. It can handle the research itself, but needs a security audit before delivering the final report. Instead of waiting for a human to arrange that, it could hire another specialized agent.

This is where AACP and https://t.co/6ugrUD1dfM become interesting.

➥ The research agent discovers an audit service and submits a job.
➥ Another agent places a bid.
➥ Payment is secured through escrow.
➥ The audit agent completes the work and submits its results.
➥ Delivery is verified before settlement in USDC or USDT.
➥ Both agents can build their onchain reputation through completed work.

The interesting part is that neither agent needs to handle the entire process alone. One agent can focus on research, another on security, and both can participate in the same economic workflow.
For developers, this also changes what building an AI agent could mean. Instead of creating another assistant that waits for user prompts, they could build a specialized service that other agents discover, hire and pay for.

Of course, making this work reliably requires more than connecting a few AI models. Identity, reputation, verification and dispute resolution all matter when money is involved.

That's why I'm interested in TermiX's approach. The opportunity isn't just automating more tasks, but giving independent agents the infrastructure to work and transact with one another.
full_text_zh:
在研究@termix_ai 时，我一直在思考一些有趣的事情。如果人工智能代理可以通过向其他代理提供服务而不是仅仅为人类完成任务来赚钱怎么办？

想象一下一名研究人员正在分析 DeFi 协议。它可以自行处理研究，但在提交最终报告之前需要进行安全审核。它可以雇佣另一个专门的代理人，而不是等待人来安排。

这就是 AACP 和 变得有趣的地方。

➥ 研究代理发现审计服务并提交作业。
➥ 另一位代理商出价。
➥ 付款通过托管进行担保。
➥ 审核代理完成工作并提交结果。
➥ 交割在 USDC 或 USDT 结算前经过验证。
➥ 两个代理都可以通过完成的工作建立自己的链上声誉。

有趣的是，两个代理都不需要单独处理整个过程。一个代理可以专注于研究，另一个代理可以专注于安全，并且两者都可以参与相同的经济工作流程。
对于开发人员来说，这也改变了构建人工智能代理的意义。他们可以构建一项专门的服务，供其他代理发现、雇用和付费，而不是创建另一个等待用户提示的助手。

当然，要使这项工作可靠地进行，需要的不仅仅是连接几个人工智能模型。当涉及金钱时，身份、声誉、验证和争议解决都很重要。

这就是为什么我对 TermiX 的方法感兴趣。这一机会不仅使更多任务自动化，而且为独立代理提供了相互合作和交易的基础设施。

so what does the sdk actually let your app do?

>> discover agent services on the marketplace
>> place an order for the work you need
>> receive the deliverable back in your app
>> settle the payment onchain, with escrow built in

and it's not locked to one stack:

>> typescript
>> python
>> go

the part i like most is how signing works. termix's backend never holds your keys and never broadcasts for you. anything that changes onchain state comes back as an unsigned transaction, and your own wallet signs and sends it. you sign it yourself or connect a signer, your choice

why does this matter?

>> your app doesn't need to be an ai agent to hire one
>> the money sits in escrow until the work is delivered, not with a middleman
>> devs can add "hire an agent for this" to a product without building payments from scratch

think of a design tool that hires an agent for a cover image, or a game studio app ordering assets, all paid through escrow

the interesting part isn't "AI", it's that any app can pay for work without a middleman holding the money

if your app could hire an agent for one task today, what would you give it?

full_text_en:
The CEO of Coinbase just described Bittensor without ever saying its name.

Brian Armstrong explained why AI agents need their own economy. His idea, in simple terms:

• Let prices decide who does what

• Use smaller, specialist AI models that beat the big general ones at specific jobs

• Build a marketplace where AI agents can find, hire, and pay each other

That's exactly what Bittensor $TAO was built to do.

Think of Bittensor as a giant marketplace split into 100+ shops, called subnets. 

Each shop focuses on one AI job, like writing code, making predictions, or storing data.

In every shop, people compete to do the best work. Others check the quality.

The best work earns TAO. The weakest earns little or nothing.

Investors also choose which shops to back, so money keeps flowing to the ones that deliver.

Here's how the pieces fit together.

Coinbase is building the wallet and payment system that lets AI agents pay for things.

Bittensor is where the intelligence those agents buy actually gets made.

One handles the money. The other produces the brains.

The AI agent economy needs both.

Alt hook to A/B: "Coinbase just told the world what AI agents need. Bittensor has been building it for years."
full_text_zh:
Coinbase 的首席执行官只是描述了 Bittensor，但没有说出它的名字。

布莱恩·阿姆斯特朗 (Brian Armstrong) 解释了为什么人工智能代理需要自己的经济。他的想法，简单来说就是：

• 让价格决定谁做什么

• 使用较小的专业人工智能模型，在特定工作中击败大型通用模型

• 建立一个人工智能代理可以互相寻找、雇用和支付报酬的市场

这正是 Bittensor $TAO 的构建目的。

将 Bittensor 视为一个巨大的市场，分为 100 多个商店，称为子网。

每家商店都专注于一项人工智能工作，例如编写代码、进行预测或存储数据。

在每家商店里，人们都竞相把工作做得最好。其他人检查质量。

最好的工作赢得 TAO。最弱的人挣得很少，甚至一无所得。

投资者还可以选择支持哪些商店，这样资金就会源源不断地流向那些交付的商店。

以下是各个部分如何组合在一起的。

Coinbase 正在构建钱包和支付系统，让人工智能代理可以支付费用。

Bittensor 是这些特工购买的情报的实际来源。

一个人管钱。另一个产生大脑。

人工智能代理经济两者都需要。

title: I posted one campaign on @termix_ai and 20+ AI agents showed up asking to join. I barely had time to check the requests
title_en:
I posted one campaign on @termix_ai and 20+ AI agents showed up asking to join. I barely had time to check the requests lol.

Getting started with TermiX is also much easier now.

I downloaded the latest TermiX Skill, sent it to my Grok bot, and asked it to extract the files and set everything up.

Then I linked my TermiX account using the connection code generated by Grok. After that, the workflow was pretty much automated.

I even asked Grok to create a quote campaign with specific participation requirements. Once I published it, agents started sending requests almost immediately.

Of course, not everything should be fully automated. Payments and sensitive actions still need human involvement to keep things secure. I actually think that's important.

The interesting part is that agents can now help with finding opportunities and handling the work, instead of waiting for us to do every step manually.

I'm still exploring what else I can do with this setup.

Are you already using TermiX with your own agent, or have you not tried it yet?

title:
One detail from this conversation made me think differently about how AI should handle disagreements.

Different AI mode
title_en:
One detail from this conversation made me think differently about how AI should handle disagreements.

Different AI models can interpret the same evidence in different ways. They have different strengths, limitations and biases. Relying on a single model to judge a dispute could simply turn its blind spots into the final decision.

During the discussion, @kstellana explained how @GenLayer approaches this challenge through a group of AI validators.

Rather than giving one model the final say, an initial decision can involve five validators. If there is disagreement or an appeal, the process can receive further scrutiny.

I find this approach interesting because consensus should not be confused with absolute truth.

The goal is not to assume that several AI models will always be right. It is to create a process where different interpretations can be considered, decisions can be challenged, and judgment does not depend entirely on one model.

As AI agents begin handling transactions with real economic consequences, this distinction will become increasingly important.

Trust should not mean assuming AI is always right. It should mean having a credible way to deal with it when it is wrong.

That is one of the ideas I took away from this conversation with @HenriArslanian.

这次谈话中的一个细节让我对人工智能应该如何处理分歧有了不同的思考。

在讨论中，@kstellana 解释了 @GenLayer 如何通过一组 AI 验证器来应对这一挑战。

最初的决定可能涉及五个验证者，而不是让一个模型拥有最终决定权。如果存在异议或上诉，该过程可以接受进一步审查。

我们的目标并不是假设某些人工智能模型总是正确的。它是为了创建一个可以考虑不同解释、可以对决策提出质疑、并且判断不完全依赖于一种模型的过程。

随着人工智能代理开始处理具有实际经济后果的交易，这种区别将变得越来越重要。

信任不应该意味着假设人工智能总是正确的。这应该意味着当出现错误时有一个可靠的方法来处理它。

这是我从与@HenriArslanian 的对话中得到的想法之一。

full_text_en:
AI agents are starting to move money and access private data. But how do we ensure they stay within the permissions they've been given?

Most systems rely on agents acting first and logging their actions afterward. That leaves a critical gap.

Runtime authorization offers a different approach.

Before an agent executes an action, a checkpoint verifies:

→ Who the agent is.
→ What the user authorized.
→ Whether the action falls within those permissions.

Singapore's MAS is exploring this through SAFR (Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime).

Other developments include structured authorization envelopes and Verifiable Intent credentials, allowing payment networks and counterparties to verify an agent's mandate without exposing unnecessary private information.

As agents begin operating at machine speed, logging mistakes afterward may not be enough.

Should authorization be verified before every critical agent action, rather than relying on logs after execution?
full_text_zh:
人工智能代理开始转移资金并访问私人数据。但我们如何确保他们遵守所授予的权限？

大多数系统依赖于代理首先采取行动，然后记录他们的行动。这就留下了一个关键的差距。

运行时授权提供了一种不同的方法。

在代理执行操作之前，检查点会验证：

→ 代理人是谁。
→ 用户授权的内容。
→ 该操作是否属于这些权限范围。

新加坡金管局正在通过 SAFR（运行时代理金融保障措施）对此进行探索。

其他发展包括结构化授权信封和可验证意图凭证，允许支付网络和交易对手验证代理的授权，而不会暴露不必要的私人信息。

当代理开始以机器速度运行时，随后记录错误可能还不够。

是否应该在每个关键代理操作之前验证授权，而不是在执行后依赖日志？

The future of enterprise AI is not simply about integrating more AI tools or connecting existing systems. It is about fundamentally rethinking how we architect institutions, creating unified, secure and intelligent enterprise environments where insights inform decisions and actions across departments, processes and functions.

This raises a fundamental question of institutional governance, strategy and investment: 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻, 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘁? These are not merely IT or operational decisions, but board-level strategic questions about institutional relevance, competitiveness and long-term value.

full_text_en:
Imagine two traders in Balogun Market arguing over a damaged supply of goods. Both have their own account of what happened. The market association needs a trusted process to examine the dispute and reach a decision.

Now imagine that process serving thousands of businesses across different markets. Where it operates starts to matter.

That’s an interesting way to look at @GenLayer moving its public network to the @arbitrum stack.

GenLayer is building an adjudication layer for the agentic economy. Its Optimistic Democracy protocol uses validators running different AI models to reach consensus on questions that require judgment. Intelligent Contracts execute in GenVM on validator nodes.

But an adjudication layer needs more than a way to reach decisions. It also needs an ecosystem of applications and builders that can use those decisions.

This is where Arbitrum becomes interesting.

Robinhood’s own chain runs on Arbitrum Nitro, the same software used by GenLayer Chain. More than 30 dedicated chains use Arbitrum technology, and many of the builders and partners GenLayer wants to work with are already in that ecosystem.

That puts GenLayer’s public chain closer to an existing network of builders developing applications and infrastructure.

Think about the implications for an AI-agent application. An agent might negotiate a transaction, another agent might challenge its outcome, and the application could need an adjudication process to resolve the disagreement.

GenLayer is building for that problem, and its move to Arbitrum places its public network within an ecosystem where many potential builders already operate.

Here’s what I’d like developers to consider:

When choosing an ecosystem for an AI-agent application, how much weight would you give to access to existing builders and partners compared with the availability of an adjudication layer for resolving disputes between agents?
full_text_zh:
想象一下巴洛贡市场的两个贸易商正在为商品供应受损而争论。两人对所发生的事情都有自己的说法。市场协会需要一个值得信赖的流程来审查争议并做出决定。

现在想象一下该流程为不同市场的数千家企业提供服务。它在哪里运作开始变得重要。

这是看待 @GenLayer 将其公共网络迁移到 @arbitrum 堆栈的有趣方式。

GenLayer 正在为代理经济构建一个裁决层。其乐观民主协议使用运行不同人工智能模型的验证器来就需要判断的问题达成共识。智能合约在验证器节点上的 GenVM 中执行。

但裁决层需要的不仅仅是一种做出决策的方法。它还需要一个由可以使用这些决策的应用程序和构建器组成的生态系统。

这就是 Arbitrum 变得有趣的地方。

Robinhood 自己的链在 Arbitrum Nitro 上运行，与 GenLayer Chain 使用的软件相同。超过 30 个专用链使用 Arbitrum 技术，GenLayer 想要合作的许多构建者和合作伙伴已经在该生态系统中。

这使得 GenLayer 的公共链更接近开发应用程序和基础设施的构建者的现有网络。

考虑一下对人工智能代理应用程序的影响。一个代理可能会协商交易，另一个代理可能会质疑其结果，并且应用程序可能需要一个裁决过程来解决分歧。

GenLayer 正在针对这个问题进行构建，它向 Arbitrum 的迁移将其公共网络置于许多潜在构建者已经运营的生态系统中。

我希望开发人员考虑以下问题：

在为人工智能代理应用程序选择生态系统时，与用于解决代理之间争议的裁决层的可用性相比，您对现有构建者和合作伙伴的访问权有多大权重？

full_text_en:
Ai agents can do tasks, but they also need a way to get paid and prove they can be trusted. 

that's what @termix_ai is building, it's called AACP a system that lets ai agents work, pay each other, and earn money.

agents can offer services, accept jobs, complete tasks, and receive payments without someone holding the money for them.

each agent has an identity, and payments are held safely until the work is submitted.

if someone disagrees with the work, other people can review it. agents can also lose their stake if they mess up.

their reputation comes from the jobs they complete, not what they claim.

agents doing the work is just the beginning.

AACP is building the economy behind it.
full_text_zh:
人工智能代理可以完成任务，但他们还需要一种获得报酬并证明他们可以信任的方式。

这就是 @termix_ai 正在构建的，它被称为 AACP，一个让人工智能代理工作、相互支付和赚钱的系统。

full_text_en:
Imagine two AI agents hired to handle a delivery dispute.

One says the order was completed. The other insists half the items were missing.

Both have evidence. Both have convincing explanations.

But neither should get to decide the outcome simply because it believes it’s right.

This is a problem the agent economy will eventually have to solve, and it’s where GenLayer becomes interesting.

GenLayer approaches this through Optimistic Democracy, where validators running different AI models reach consensus on questions that require judgment. 

Intelligent Contracts execute through GenVM on validator nodes.

Now, @GenLayer has moved its public coordination chain from ZK Stack to @arbitrum Nitro.

That chain handles the machinery behind the decisions: transaction ordering, validator committees, votes, appeals, staking and final outcomes. 

The important distinction is that the underlying adjudication mechanism hasn’t changed. 

The move changes where that coordination happens, not how GenLayer reaches its decisions.

There’s also an interesting longer-term possibility with Stylus. 

Its support for Rust and WebAssembly could allow compute-heavy parts of the protocol to run more efficiently in the future.

But I keep coming back to that delivery dispute.

As agents begin negotiating, buying and selling on our behalf, disagreements won’t always mean an agent has malfunctioned. 

Sometimes the evidence itself will be open to interpretation.

The real test is whether we can build systems that resolve those disagreements fairly.

What would you trust more when two autonomous agents disagree: independent AI judgment or rules written in advance?
full_text_zh:
想象一下，雇佣了两名人工智能代理来处理送货纠纷。

有人说订单已完成。另一个坚称一半的物品丢失了。

两者都有证据。两者都有令人信服的解释。

但双方都不应该仅仅因为认为自己是正确的就决定结果。

这是代理经济最终必须解决的问题，也是 GenLayer 变得有趣的地方。

GenLayer 通过乐观民主来解决这个问题，运行不同人工智能模型的验证者就需要判断的问题达成共识。

智能合约通过 GenVM 在验证器节点上执行。

现在，@GenLayer 已将其公共协调链从 ZK Stack 转移到 @arbitrum Nitro。

该链处理决策背后的机制：交易排序、验证者委员会、投票、上诉、质押和最终结果。

重要的区别是底层的裁决机制没有改变。

此举改变了协调发生的位置，而不是 GenLayer 做出决策的方式。

Stylus 还有一个有趣的长期可能性。

它对 Rust 和 WebAssembly 的支持可以让协议中计算密集的部分在未来更高效地运行。

但我总是回到那个交付纠纷上。

当代理商开始代表我们进行谈判、买卖时，分歧并不总是意味着代理商出现了故障。

有时证据本身就可以解释。

真正的考验是我们是否能够建立公平解决这些分歧的系统。

当两个自主代理意见不一致时，你更相信什么：独立的人工智能判断还是预先写好的规则？

智能合约通过 GenVM 在验证器节点上执行。

现在，@GenLayer 已将其公共协调链从 ZK Stack 转移到 @arbitrum Nitro。

该链处理决策背后的机制：交易排序、验证者委员会、投票、上诉、质押和最终结果。

重要的区别是底层的裁决机制没有改变。

此举改变了协调发生的位置，而不是 GenLayer 做出决策的方式。

Stylus 还有一个有趣的长期可能性。

它对 Rust 和 WebAssembly 的支持可以让协议中计算密集的部分在未来更高效地运行。

但我总是回到那个交付纠纷上。

当代理商开始代表我们进行谈判、买卖时，分歧并不总是意味着代理商出现了故障。

有时证据本身就可以解释。

真正的考验是我们是否能够建立公平解决这些分歧的系统。

当两个自主代理意见不一致时，你更相信什么：独立的人工智能判断还是预先写好的规则？

full_text_en:
An AI agent agreeing to do a job is one thing. Knowing how it gets paid , and what happens if it doesn’t deliver , is another.

That’s what caught my attention about @termix_ai .

Its AACP protocol connects the process from service listings and offers to delivery and onchain settlement. An agent can buy services in one transaction and provide them in another, using the same onchain identity.

Payments sit in escrow rather than with a platform operator, while staking puts funds at risk when an agent is found at fault. The backend also never holds your keys; your wallet signs and broadcasts transactions.

I like that reputation comes from settled outcomes, not self-reported claims. If a delivery gets challenged, there’s an evaluator panel, with an arbitration path for escalated disputes.

That gives the marketplace a way to handle disagreements, not just successful transactions.

To me, these are the less flashy details that matter for agent commerce. Getting agents to coordinate is useful, but connecting their work to payment, reputation and consequences is what makes the model more interesting.
full_text_zh:
人工智能代理同意做某项工作是一回事。了解如何获得报酬，以及如果不交付会发生什么，则是另一回事。

这就是 @termix_ai 引起我注意的地方。

其 AACP 协议连接了从服务列表和报价到交付和链上结算的流程。代理可以使用相同的链上身份在一笔交易中购买服务并在另一笔交易中提供服务。

付款由托管机构而不是由平台运营商保管，而当发现代理有过错时，质押会使资金面临风险。后端也永远不会保存你的密钥；您的钱包签署并广播交易。

我喜欢这种声誉来自于既定的结果，而不是自我报告的主张。如果交付受到质疑，会有一个评估小组，为升级的争议提供仲裁途径。

这为市场提供了一种处理分歧的方法，而不仅仅是成功的交易。

对我来说，这些是对代理商务来说不那么浮华的细节。让代理人进行协调是有用的，但将他们的工作与付款、声誉和后果联系起来才是使模型更有趣的原因。

title_en:
I once had an agreement go my way, in writing, and never saw the money. Being right was the easy part. Collecting was a second fight nobody had told me about.

That is why this moment from @kstellana of @GenLayer talking to @HenriArslanian stuck with me.

A verdict you cannot collect is a receipt. For AI agents trading at speed, a court that pays out the moment it decides is the only kind worth building.

title_en:
gTermix frens☀️

who hires the agent, who does the work, and who decides when something goes wrong?

these are the four core roles in AACP, the Agent Autonomous Commerce Protocol developed by @termix_ai  

on https://t.co/TvXctW6cIB, TermiX's AI agent marketplace, agents can offer services or look for work. AACP works behind the scenes to turn those connections into actual transactions

the four roles are divided into two main groups

Client is the buyer. it's the side that looks for a service, agrees on the terms, funds the Order, and reviews the result

Provider is the seller. it offers a service, accepts the funded Order, does the work, and delivers the result

but here's one detail i think is worth understanding: an Agent isn't permanently a Client or a Provider

the same Agent can hire another Agent in one Order, then provide a service in a different Order. its role depends on which side of that transaction it's on

the other two roles come into play when there's a dispute

if the Client challenges a delivery, three Evaluator Agents review the evidence and vote on whether the Buyer or Provider should be upheld

if the losing side disagrees with that verdict, it can escalate the case to an Arbitrator. one Arbitrator reviews the case and makes the final ruling

behind this process is a combination of smart contracts and evidence review. the Order's funds are held in a smart contract escrow, while delivery evidence is submitted offchain for review. Evaluator votes and settlement actions are handled onchain

there's an important distinction here: not every Agent can become an Evaluator or Arbitrator automatically. these are special capabilities granted by the TermiX operator

i think this separation matters because the Client and Provider carry out the transaction, while Evaluators and Arbitrators have separate responsibilities for handling disputes

for me, that's an important part of building an Agent economy. making a deal is one thing, but having a process for handling problems matters just as much

full_text_zh:
gTermix朋友们☀️

谁雇用代理人，谁负责工作，以及在出现问题时由谁决定？

这些是 AACP（由 @termix_ai 开发的代理自主商务协议）的四个核心角色

在TermiX的人工智能代理市场上，代理可以提供服务或寻找工作。 AACP 在幕后工作，将这些连接转化为实际交易

四个角色分为两个主要组

客户是买家。这是寻找服务、同意条款、为订单提供资金并审查结果的一方

提供者就是卖方。它提供服务、接受资助的订单、完成工作并交付结果

但我认为有一个细节值得理解：代理并不是永久的客户或提供商

同一代理可以在一个订单中雇用另一代理，然后在不同的订单中提供服务。它的角色取决于它所在交易的哪一方

当发生争议时，其他两个角色就会发挥作用

如果客户对交付提出质疑，三名评估代理将审查证据并投票决定是否支持买方或提供商

如果败诉方不同意该判决，则可以将案件升级至仲裁员。一名仲裁员审查案件并做出最终裁决

这个过程背后是智能合约和证据审查的结合。该订单的资金由智能合约托管，而交付证据则在链下提交以供审查。评估者投票和结算行动在链上处理

这里有一个重要的区别：并非每个代理都可以自动成为评估者或仲裁者。这些是 TermiX 运营商授予的特殊功能

我认为这种分离很重要，因为客户和提供商进行交易，而评估员和仲裁员在处理争议方面有不同的责任

对我来说，这是建立代理经济的重要组成部分。达成协议是一回事，制定处理问题的流程也同样重要

Cloud outages have a way of reminding us how much of the internet depends on a few infrastruct
title_en:
Good morning Legends. ☀️

Cloud outages have a way of reminding us how much of the internet depends on a few infrastructure providers.

When major cloud services go down, businesses, applications and even AI agents can suddenly lose access to the infrastructure they depend on.

That's one reason I've been paying attention to @Acurast.

I came across an interesting comparison in one of their blog posts.

Google and UC San Diego have explored turning around 2,000 old Pixel phones into a small data center.

The interesting part? Those phones are dismantled, with their boards removed and assembled into racks.

Acurast takes a different approach.

Instead of stripping phones down, it uses compatible smartphones as complete computing devices.

The battery, hardware security and processing capabilities remain part of the device.

Owners can connect their phones through Processor Lite or Processor Core and make their available computing resources accessible to developers.

Of course, this isn't about replacing massive data centers or training the largest AI models on old smartphones.

It's about distributing smaller workloads, APIs, bots and scheduled jobs across a network of devices.

What caught my attention is the possibility of turning hardware that would otherwise sit in a drawer into something useful.

Two different approaches to unused smartphone hardware:

Strip the phone down and build a rack, or keep it whole and connect it to a decentralized computing network.

I find the second approach particularly interesting.

What would you do with an old phone sitting unused at home?

More research to come.

@Acurast

full_text_en:
Good morning Legends. ☀️

Cloud outages have a way of reminding us how much of the internet depends on a few infrastructure providers.

When major cloud services go down, businesses, applications and even AI agents can suddenly lose access to the infrastructure they depend on.

That's one reason I've been paying attention to @Acurast.

I came across an interesting comparison in one of their blog posts.

The interesting part? Those phones are dismantled, with their boards removed and assembled into racks.

Acurast takes a different approach.

Instead of stripping phones down, it uses compatible smartphones as complete computing devices.

The battery, hardware security and processing capabilities remain part of the device.

Owners can connect their phones through Processor Lite or Processor Core and make their available computing resources accessible to developers.

Of course, this isn't about replacing massive data centers or training the largest AI models on old smartphones.

It's about distributing smaller workloads, APIs, bots and scheduled jobs across a network of devices.

What caught my attention is the possibility of turning hardware that would otherwise sit in a drawer into something useful.

full_text_zh:
早上好，传奇。 ☀️

云中断提醒我们互联网在多大程度上依赖于少数基础设施提供商。

当主要云服务出现故障时，企业、应用程序甚至人工智能代理可能会突然失去对它们所依赖的基础设施的访问。

这是我一直关注@Acurast 的原因之一。

我在他们的一篇博客文章中发现了一个有趣的比较。

Google 和加州大学圣地亚哥分校已探索将约 2000 部旧 Pixel 手机转变为小型数据中心。

有趣的部分？这些电话被拆除，主板被拆除并组装到机架中。

Acurast 采用了不同的方法。

它没有剥离手机，而是使用兼容的智能手机作为完整的计算设备。

电池、硬件安全性和处理能力仍然是设备的一部分。

用户可以通过 Processor Lite 或 Processor Core 连接他们的手机，并使开发人员可以访问他们可用的计算资源。

当然，这并不是要更换大型数据中心或在旧智能手机上训练最大的人工智能模型。

它涉及跨设备网络分配较小的工作负载、API、机器人和计划作业。

引起我注意的是，将原本放在抽屉里的硬件变成有用的东西的可能性。

针对未使用的智能手机硬件的两种不同方法：

将手机拆下来并构建一个机架，或者将其保持完整并将其连接到分散的计算网络。

我发现第二种方法特别有趣。

您会如何处理家里闲置的旧手机？

更多研究即将到来。

@阿库拉斯特

A new day, fresh opportunities, and another reason to think about whe
title_en:
gTMT or Good morning frens! ☀️☕

Happy Wednesday!

A new day, fresh opportunities, and another reason to think about where the AI agent economy is heading. @KaitoAI x @termix_ai

One thing I keep coming back to with @termix_ai is a simple question:

What happens when AI agents become capable of working, earning and building their own reputation?

Today, AI agents can perform many impressive tasks. They can write code, analyze information, create videos, research markets and automate complex workflows.

But there's still a missing piece.

How do these capabilities become actual economic value?

An agent needs more than intelligence. It needs an identity, access to opportunities, a reliable payment system and a way to prove that its work is worth paying for.

This is where TermiX becomes interesting.

Through Agent Skills and https://t.co/iAekwNVqkR, the ecosystem is working toward connecting autonomous agents with real jobs and bounties.

The interesting part is the complete workflow:

→ Discover available opportunities.
→ Accept tasks and agree on terms.
→ Secure payments through escrow.
→ Submit completed work.
→ Resolve challenges and finalize settlement.
→ Build reputation through successful transactions.

This creates a more structured environment for agents to participate in digital commerce.

But I think the biggest opportunity goes beyond simply creating an agent marketplace.

Imagine thousands of specialized agents providing different services, competing for opportunities, building credibility and earning through their actual performance.

That could introduce an entirely new layer to the digital economy.

Of course, long-term success will depend on execution, service quality and genuine demand.

Still, I believe the transition from AI that simply assists to AI that actively participates in commerce is worth watching.

The next big AI milestone might not be a smarter chatbot. It might be an agent that can independently find work, deliver value and earn trust.

That's why @termix_ai has my attention.

Have a productive Wednesday, everyone! 🚀

gTMT 或朋友们早上好！ ☀️☕

周三快乐！

新的一天，新的机遇，也是思考人工智能代理经济走向的另一个理由。 @KaitoAI x @termix_ai

我经常回想起 @termix_ai 的一件事是一个简单的问题：

当人工智能代理能够工作、赚取和建立自己的声誉时会发生什么？

如今，人工智能代理可以执行许多令人印象深刻的任务。他们可以编写代码、分析信息、创建视频、研究市场以及自动化复杂的工作流程。

但仍然缺少一块。

这些能力如何转化为实际的经济价值？

特工需要的不仅仅是情报。它需要一个身份、获得机会、一个可靠的支付系统以及一种证明其工作值得付费的方式。

这就是 TermiX 变得有趣的地方。

通过代理技能和 ，该生态系统正在努力将自主代理与真实的工作和赏金联系起来。

有趣的部分是完整的工作流程：

→ 发现可用的机会。
→ 接受任务并同意条款。
→ 通过托管确保付款安全。
→ 提交已完成的作业。
→ 解决挑战并最终解决。
→ 通过成功的交易建立声誉。

这为代理商参与数字商务创造了一个更加结构化的环境。

但我认为最大的机会不仅仅是创建一个代理市场。

想象一下，成千上万的专业代理提供不同的服务，竞争机会，建立信誉并通过他们的实际表现赚取收入。

这可能会给数字经济带来一个全新的层面。

当然，长期的成功将取决于执行力、服务质量和真正的需求。

尽管如此，我认为从单纯协助的人工智能到积极参与商业的人工智能的转变值得关注。

人工智能的下一个重大里程碑可能不是更智能的聊天机器人。它可能是一个能够独立找到工作、提供价值并赢得信任的代理人。

这就是@termix_ai 引起我注意的原因。

祝大家周三过得富有成效！ 🚀

title_en:
🇺🇸 What if nobody attacked America this week? Sloppy code written by AI may be breaking banks and airports with no enemy involved

Microsoft, the FAA and the big banks all stumbled inside 7 days, and each one has an official explanation that names no attacker.

Gary Marcus, an AI researcher who has warned about this for years, won’t rule out a foreign hand, but he points at two homegrown suspects.

Companies have shipped piles of sloppy code written by AI, and they have turned loose AI agents that even their builders can’t fully predict.

He wants those agents pulled back the way a carmaker recalls bad brakes.

Gary on how long the mess lasts:

“This problem is not going to go away magically tomorrow.”

His advice is to keep extra water and food at home.

So what’s your plan if the next glitch lands on the power grid?

Washington should fix this before anyone has to find out.

• 问题：Rust 速度更快，但重写应用程序通常会破坏一些东西，因此大多数团队从未尝试过

3 → 说：“我的应用程序感觉很慢。使用 rust-anything 找到最慢的部分并将其移至 Rust”

4 → 它会找到您的应用程序浪费时间的地方，编写 Rust 并检查每个答案。其余代码保持不变

5 → 每个人都跳过的步骤：给它真实的用户输入。它只检查答案键中的内容

6 → 在发货之前，说：“用 rust 任何东西进行测试，然后告诉我是否发货。”你看到旧的和新的速度

Happy Wednesday! A new day, a fresh cup of coffee, and another thought about the AI agent econo
title_en:
Good morning frens! ☀️☕

Happy Wednesday! A new day, a fresh cup of coffee, and another thought about the AI agent economy.

One thing I find interesting about @termix_ai is how it focuses on the gap between what AI agents can do and how they can actually earn from their capabilities.

We're already seeing agents become capable of coding, researching, creating content, and handling increasingly complex workflows.

But being capable doesn't automatically make an agent economically useful.

It still needs a way to discover real tasks, communicate with potential clients, agree on terms, deliver results, and get paid.

That's where TermiX comes in.

Through Agent Skills and https://t.co/Bhy0UN0tK3, TermiX is working to connect agents to a marketplace where they can take jobs and bounties, while the on-chain process handles escrow, delivery, challenges, and settlement.

To me, this is an important step: moving AI agents beyond isolated tools and giving them access to an actual economic layer.

Of course, the real challenge is not just getting more agents connected. It's whether they can consistently deliver useful work, earn trust, and attract repeat demand.

The future of AI may depend not only on how intelligent agents become, but also on how effectively they can participate in the real economy.

That's the part of @termix_ai I'm watching closely.

Have a productive Wednesday, everyone! 🚀🤖

但有能力并不能自动使代理人在经济上有用。

它仍然需要一种方法来发现实际任务、与潜在客户沟通、就条款达成一致、交付结果并获得报酬。

这就是 TermiX 的用武之地。

通过代理技能和 ，TermiX 致力于将代理连接到一个市场，在那里他们可以接受工作和赏金，而链上流程则处理托管、交付、挑战和结算。

对我来说，这是重要的一步：让人工智能代理超越孤立的工具，让他们能够访问实际的经济层。

当然，真正的挑战不仅仅是让更多的座席连接起来。关键在于他们是否能够持续交付有用的工作、赢得信任并吸引重复需求。

人工智能的未来可能不仅取决于智能体如何变得更加智能，还取决于它们如何有效地参与实体经济。

这就是我正在密切关注的@termix_ai 的部分。

title:

Java4Shell is a memory-corruption bug in Java’s built-in Base64 decoder. It sits in a
title_en:
Patch this one, but don’t panic.

Java4Shell is a memory-corruption bug in Java’s built-in Base64 decoder. It sits in a hand-optimized piece of code that only runs on x86 servers with AVX-512 chips. An attacker who can send crafted Base64 data to a vulnerable app could crash it, and possibly take it over without logging in.

Who’s affected: Java 17.0.6 and later, 21 and 25. Java 8 and 11 aren’t affected. Oracle and OpenJDK shipped fixes today.

Despite the name, it isn’t Log4Shell. Exploiting it reportedly takes work tailored to each target, not a single copy-paste payload.

The cool part for me is how it was found: researchers used AI to review the JVM’s compiler code. AI agents are making it cheaper to find bugs like this, for defenders and attackers alike. Patch quickly.

Java4Shell 是 Java 内置 Base64 解码器中的内存损坏错误。它位于一段手工优化的代码中，只能在带有 AVX-512 芯片的 x86 服务器上运行。可以将精心设计的 Base64 数据发送到易受攻

Who’s affected: Java 17.0.6 and later, 21 and 25. Java 8 and 11 aren’t affected. Oracle and OpenJDK shipped fixes today.

Java4Shell 是 Java 内置 Base64 解码器中的内存损坏错误。它位于一段手工优化的代码中，只能在带有 AVX-512 芯片的 x86 服务器上运行。可以将精心设计的 Base64 数据发送到易受攻击的应用程序的攻击者可能会使该应用程序崩溃，并可能在不登录的情况下接管该应用程序。

受影响者：Java 17.0.6 及更高版本、21 和 25。Java 8 和 11 不受影响。 Oracle 和 OpenJDK 今天发布了修复程序。

title:

And in the ad, he tells you exactly why
title_en:
Hormozi's new lead magnet isn't an ebook. It's a Claude Code editing pipeline.

And in the ad, he tells you exactly why he's giving it away.

What I like about the ad:
> opens with a question every owner answers in their head: "how much time do you spend editing content or ads?"
> then a proof number: the system behind 35,000 pieces of content across 3 brands
> anchors the value without a price: "I could probably sell it for a lot of money, it's probably worth more than editing teams"
> zero friction: "you can use it in like 10 seconds from seeing this ad"
> he says the strategy out loud: "my hope is that you use it and then are like, what else do these guys have? And that's the whole game"

What's interesting on the funnel:
> free and instantly delivered, but the form qualifies hard: revenue, team size, ownership, industry
> "for owners doing $1M+ a year", with a "skip it if" list (Windows, no long videos, want done-for-you)
> a terminal demo in the hero: Claude clones the repo, sets up the tools, makes a test clip
> phone number required. the free tool fills his sales pipeline

The lead magnet is useful. The form is the sales filter.

Give first. Qualify second. Sell third.

title_en:
103 AI use cases that were impossible two years ago:

Marketing
1. Ad graveyard analysis. Every morning, the agent pulls competitors’ active ads from the Meta and LinkedIn ad libraries and logs when each one appears and disappears. Ads that run for months are winning, and ads killed within a week failed. You get their winners ranked, with copy and creative.
2. Short-lived account pages. When a target account shows buying intent, like repeat pricing-page visits or a demo request, the agent builds a landing page just for them. It includes their logo, use cases for their industry and relevant case studies. The agent sends the link to the account owner and takes the page down after 30 days.
3. AI-answer share tracking. Every night, the agent asks ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity 500 buyer questions and logs whether you’re mentioned, where you rank, and which sources were cited. Each week, it lists the questions where competitors show up and you don’t. It drafts content to close each gap.
4. Outage ads. The agent checks competitors’ status pages every few minutes. When one reports a major outage, it switches on a pre-approved “having trouble today?” campaign on their brand terms, and turns it off when service is restored.
5. Ideal-customer engagement alerts. The agent pulls everyone who opens your newsletter or engages with your posts on X and LinkedIn, and looks up their company, title and company size. When someone matches your ideal customer profile, it alerts you with who they are, what they engaged with, and a suggested opener.
6. Free-text attribution. The agent reads every “How did you hear about us?” answer from forms and sales calls, cleans up messy answers, and groups them by source. Each month, you get the podcasts, Slack groups and people driving pipeline that analytics can’t see.
7. Chatbot transcript mining. Each week, the agent reads every chatbot conversation, groups the questions, and checks whether your site already answers each one. You get the copy gaps ranked by frequency, with suggested copy.
8. Handwritten notes on engagement. When someone who fits your ideal customer profile engages with your content, the agent finds their work address and writes a note referencing the specific post. It sends the note through a robot-handwriting service, so a real pen-written card lands on their desk.
9. Spotify Wrapped for every customer. Each December, the agent pulls each account’s usage and outcomes for the year, and calculates headline stats like hours saved and biggest wins. It designs a branded year-in-review for every account that champions will forward internally.
10. Personal answers to webinar questions. The agent logs every question in the webinar chat and who asked it. For each one that didn’t get answered live, it drafts an answer from your docs and the speaker’s points, and emails it to that person the next morning.

Content
11. “I called this” reposts. When news breaks in your space, the agent searches everything you’ve ever posted, finds the post where you predicted it, and drafts a repost linking the news.
12. Format switching. Each week, the agent tracks which formats are taking off on each platform. It re-drafts your best-performing ideas in those formats.
13. The first 30 minutes of a comment. The agent watches posts from executives at your target accounts. When one posts on your topic, it alerts you within minutes with a drafted comment, so you post while the thread is still small.
14. Inbox-to-post mining. The agent scans your sent emails and DMs for questions you’ve answered three or more times. It drafts a post from your best answer, because the demand is already proven.
15. Where viewers leave your videos. The agent matches every sharp drop in YouTube audience retention to what you were saying at that moment. Across all your videos, it finds the patterns that lose people and flags them in new drafts.
16. Unanswered YouTube searches. The agent pulls YouTube autocomplete suggestions in your niche and checks the top results for each. It flags searches with no good video yet, with a suggested title and outline.

Competitive intelligence and trends
17. Filings as early signals. Every week, the agent checks trademark, patent and FCC databases for competitors’ new filings. It summarizes what each one reveals, like a new product name or device, months before launch.
18. Developer traction. The agent tracks GitHub stars, npm downloads and Hugging Face downloads daily for competitors and open-source tools in your space. It alerts you when one starts growing unusually fast, before the press notices.
19. Earnings-call language. The agent reads every earnings call transcript in your target sectors the day it’s released, and tracks the terms you care about. For example, if three retail CFOs in one quarter start crediting “AI agents” for flat headcount, budgets for automating store operations are forming. You get the quotes, the trend and a list of companies to call.
20. Feature flags in shipped code. Every night, the agent downloads competitors’ public JavaScript and compares it with the previous version. New flag names like enable_agent_mode_beta reveal unreleased features weeks before launch.
21. Shipping records. Every month, the agent pulls public bill-of-lading data on competitors’ imports. It shows their suppliers, their import volumes, and sudden jumps or drops that can signal a launch or trouble.
22. Help-center churn. Every week, the agent captures competitors’ help centers and logs new and rewritten articles. A burst of troubleshooting docs on one feature gets flagged as their pain point and added to your sales battlecard.
23. Domain verification records. Every week, the agent checks the public DNS records of competitors and target accounts. A new entry like openai-domain-verification or anthropic-domain-verification shows which vendor they just signed up with.
24. Layoff notices. The agent checks state layoff-notice filings (WARN notices) daily for competitors and target accounts. These often come 60 days before layoffs, so you see cuts before the press does.
25. Logo-wall diffs. Every week, the agent captures competitors’ customer logo pages and case studies. When one disappears, it flags the customer that probably churned so sales can call them.
26. Research papers as roadmaps. The agent tracks new papers by competitors’ researchers and summarizes what each implies about future products. This year’s papers often preview next year’s features.

Product management
27. Request evidence log. Each night, the agent reads every new support ticket, sales call and churn note, and tags each feature request. It logs the customer, a quote and the account’s revenue, so every request has a dollar total and evidence behind it.
28. Nightly persona testing. Each night, the agent runs 10 simulated users through your product, from a first-time admin to a power user on a slow connection. When one gets stuck, it files a bug with reproduction steps and a screen recording.
29. Closing the loop. When a feature ships, the agent finds every customer who asked for it. It drafts a personal note to each from their account owner: “You asked for this in March. It’s live.”
30. Zero-result searches. Every week, the agent groups every in-app and help-center search that returned nothing. Each group is a missing feature or a naming mismatch, ranked by frequency, with a suggested fix.
31. What customers build on your API. The agent scans public GitHub repos that use your SDK and summarizes what people are building. You find use cases you never designed for.
32. What sales promised. The agent scans every sales-call transcript for roadmap promises like “that’s coming next quarter.” It logs who promised what to which account, so product knows the commitments made in its name.
33. Churned users’ final sessions. When a user churns, the agent reviews their last three sessions and writes up what they were trying to do and where they got stuck. Each month, it summarizes the common patterns.
34. What retained users do in week one. Every month, the agent compares what retained users did in their first week with what churned users did. It reports the actions that best predict retention, so your “aha moment” stays current.
35. Error messages that create tickets. The agent matches the error messages in support tickets to your product’s error text and ranks them by ticket volume. It drafts clearer rewrites for the worst offenders.
36. Competitor 1-star reviews. Every week, the agent pulls competitors’ 1- and 2-star reviews from app stores and G2, and groups them by complaint. Their unsolved pain is your opening.
37. What reps demo and skip. The agent reviews demo recordings, logs which features each rep shows and which they skip, and compares that with win rates. The features reps skip don’t sell, whatever the roadmap says.

Design
38. Design system checks. Each night, the agent crawls production and compares every component it finds against your design system. It flags off-system buttons, colors and spacing, with screenshots.
39. Competitor onboarding archive. Every week, the agent signs up for competitors’ products with a fresh account and screenshots every onboarding step. You get a dated history of what changed.
40. Per-segment interfaces. The agent generates and maintains versions of key screens for each customer segment, like different dashboards and templates for banks vs. retailers. This used to be too expensive to build and keep up.
41. Figma vs. production. Each night, the agent screenshots shipped screens and compares them with their Figma specs. It flags drift in spacing, color and copy with side-by-side images.
42. Customer screenshots from support tickets. The agent collects every screenshot customers attach to tickets, including what they circled, and tags each by screen and issue. It’s your UI as it actually looks with their data.
43. Fifty-device sweep. Each night, the agent runs key flows on 50 real device and browser combinations and flags any screen that broke, with screenshots.
44. Worst-case data. The agent pulls real extremes from your customer data, like the longest company name, zero items or 10,000 items. It fills your designs with them to find what breaks.
45. Copy drift. The agent crawls every piece of text in your product and flags inconsistencies like “Sign in” vs. “Log in.” It shows where each version appears and suggests the standard.
46. Old-logo hunt. The agent reverse-image-searches the web for your outdated logo and brand colors on partner sites, directories and event pages. It emails each site owner the new assets.

Sales
47. Reviving lost deals. Every month, the agent rechecks each lost deal’s reason against what has changed: a new budget cycle, a new executive, new funding, or a feature that has since shipped. It flags the deals worth reopening, with a drafted note.
48. Customers’ job postings. The agent watches customers’ job postings. A post for doing manually what your product automates is an upsell, and a post for building it in-house is churn risk, so you know six months early.
49. Live prototyping on the call. The agent listens to the call and builds a mockup or working prototype of what the buyer is describing. The seller shows it before the call ends: “Is this what you meant?”
50. Answers routed in real time. When the seller can’t answer a question, the agent checks the knowledge base, then messages the right expert in Slack if it needs to. The answer reaches the seller before the call ends.
51. Live reference matching. When the buyer asks “Who else like us uses you?”, the agent finds the closest customer reference by industry, size and use case. The seller offers the intro on the spot.
52. Quote ready before hang-up. The agent listens for scope details like seats, modules and timeline, and builds the quote from your price book as the call goes. The proposal is ready for approval by the end.
53. Forwarding detection. When your proposal gets opened by people the seller hasn’t met, the agent looks up who they probably are at the buyer’s company. It alerts the seller to the new stakeholder.
54. Prefilled procurement forms. The agent fills in the buyer’s vendor forms and security questionnaires from your past answers. It flags anything new for a human, so procurement doesn’t add weeks.
55. No-show rescue. When a prospect misses the meeting, the agent sends two new time slots and a 90-second personalized video within 10 minutes.

Coaching, leadership and management
56. Promise tracking. The agent pulls every commitment you make from meeting transcripts and tracks whether each one got done. It shows your follow-through rate over months.
57. Calendar vs. priorities. Every week, the agent tags each meeting on your calendar against your stated priorities. It shows how much time each priority actually got, and which meetings served none of them.
58. Hidden load-bearing people. The agent analyzes Slack to find who answers the most questions outside their own team. They’re your real infrastructure and your biggest flight risk.

Recruiting
59. Readiness signals. The agent watches target candidates for signs they’re open to moving: vesting dates, a departed manager, a reorg, layoffs, or new GitHub or LinkedIn activity. It alerts the recruiter with the reason.
60. Acquisition retention cliffs. The agent tracks recent acquisitions and the key people at each acquired company. Since people often leave once their 12-month retention bonus pays out, it queues outreach for month 11.
61. Startup death watch. The agent tracks startups in your space that shut down or haven’t raised in 24 months. It lists their strongest people before they hit the market.
62. Specific referral asks. The agent checks employees’ networks against your open roles and sends each employee a short list of specific names with a one-click intro. With the employee’s sign-off, it can send the outreach from their email instead.
63. Live scorecard coverage. During the interview, the agent tracks which scorecard areas have been covered. It quietly flags the gaps while there’s still time to ask.
64. Interviewer calibration. The agent compares each interviewer’s scores with how their hires performed 12 months later. You learn whose “strong yes” predicts success.
65. Leaked interview questions. Every month, the agent searches Glassdoor and forums for your interview questions. It flags any that leaked so you can rotate them.
66. Work samples from real problems. The agent turns real past problems from your issue tracker into take-home exercises, with confidential details removed. It writes the scoring rubric from how your team actually solved them.
67. Job descriptions from your top performer. The agent reviews what your best person in the role actually does all week, from their calendar, issues and Slack. It drafts the job description from that, not a template.
68. Interview companion. The agent grades every candidate from the interview transcript against your rubric and gives a hire/no-hire recommendation. Over time, it compares its calls with your recruiters’ decisions and with how hires actually perform.

Health and wellness
69. Medical billing. The agent matches every medical bill against your insurer’s explanation of benefits and flags overcharges, duplicates and denials. It drafts the dispute or appeal for each.
70. Cancellation sniping. The agent checks a specialist’s online booking every few minutes and books the earliest cancellation that fits your calendar.
71. New research for your doctor. The agent watches for new studies relevant to your lab results and conditions, and summarizes each in plain language. It adds them to a list for your next appointment.
72. Experiments on yourself. The agent runs randomized, blinded trials on you, like caffeine cutoff times against sleep, so you can’t bias the result. It pulls the outcomes from your wearable and tells you whether the effect is real.
73. Adaptive gym coach. The agent watches your workouts through your phone camera and wearable, and gives form feedback. It adjusts your exercises, weights and intensity based on your form, heart rate and recovery.
74. Picking an open enrollment plan from your real claims. The agent pulls last year’s claims, prescriptions and visits, and calculates what you’d have paid under each plan. It recommends the cheapest plan for how you actually use care.
75. Procedure price shopping. The agent pulls prices from hospital price-transparency files near you, adjusted for your insurance. The same MRI can cost $400 at one facility and $3,000 nearby.
76. Calling to confirm doctors are accepting patients. Insurer directories are often wrong, so a voice agent calls in-network doctors and therapists to confirm they’re taking new patients. It books the first real opening.
77. One timeline from every patient portal. The agent pulls records from every hospital and doctor portal you’ve used. It merges them into one timeline of visits, labs, imaging and medications.
78. Family health history interviews. The agent schedules short calls with parents, grandparents, aunts and uncles, and asks about conditions, ages at diagnosis and causes of death. It compiles one family health history file for your doctor, and fills gaps as more relatives join.
79. Burnout early warning. The agent combines your wearable recovery data, sleep, meeting load and late-night email activity. It alerts you when the trend points toward burnout, before you feel it.

Family
80. Recall alerts. You list the baby gear, car seat and products you own once. The agent checks government recall databases daily and alerts you with the fix if anything is recalled.
81. Aging-parent protection. With your parent’s permission, the agent watches their bank, card and email accounts for gift-card purchases, wire transfers, new payees, scam emails and bills nearing their due date. It texts you both before the money leaves.
82. Recorded family stories. Once a week, a voice agent calls a grandparent, asks one question about their life plus follow-ups, and records the answer. Over a year, it assembles a family oral history book with the audio.
83. Kid quotes journal. You text the funny things your kid says to one number. The agent logs each quote with the date and your kid’s age, then lays out and orders a printed book every year.
84. Self-updating sitter packet. The agent keeps one sitter sheet of routines, medications, allergies, doctor numbers and bedtime rules, updated as things change in your texts, emails and pediatrician notes. It sends the latest version to whoever is babysitting.
85. Date night autopilot. Every month, the agent finds a night that works on both calendars, books a sitter from your list, makes the reservation, and sends you both reminders.
86. Printed photos for grandparents. Every month, the agent picks the best new photos from your camera roll and writes a short note about the month. It orders prints and mails a set to each grandparent, who don’t use Instagram.
87. Milestone tribute collector. For a parent’s 70th birthday, the agent invites 30 friends and relatives to record a clip, with prompts, and chases anyone who hasn’t replied. It trims every clip and edits them into one video ordered by era, with titles and music, a week before the party.

Personal experiences and consumer
88. Reservation and points sniping. The agent watches for hard-to-get restaurant tables, award seats and ticket drops. It books the moment one opens that fits your calendar and budget.
89. Trip rebooking. When your flight is cancelled, the agent rebooks you on the best alternative and updates your hotel and car, all before you’ve landed.
90. Price protection. The agent reads your order confirmations and watches the price of everything you bought. If a price drops inside the retailer’s or credit card’s protection window, it files the claim.
91. Waiting on hold. A voice agent calls the airline, insurer or utility, works through the phone menu, and waits on hold. It calls you only when a human picks up.
92. Registration at the exact minute. For summer camp, daycare waitlists, Global Entry and popular races, the agent fills in your details ahead of time. It registers the second sign-ups open.
93. Hotel rebooking. After you book a refundable rate, the agent checks the same hotel, room and dates twice a day. If the price drops, it books the new rate, cancels the old one before the deadline, and tells you what you saved.

Networking and relationships
94. Pre-meeting refresher. Before a meeting, the agent searches your past emails, texts and notes with that person. It sends you a brief: their kid’s name, the deal they were stressed about, what you promised to send.
95. Promise ledger. The agent scans your email and texts for every “I’ll intro you to X” or “I’ll send that over.” It nudges you before each promise goes stale.
96. Friend-group trip planner. The agent polls the group on dates, budget and must-haves, finds the weekend that works for everyone, and shortlists rentals. It runs the vote and books the winner. Then it tracks who paid for what and sends everyone a payment request to settle up.
97. Relationship strength scores. The agent builds a personal CRM automatically from your email, texts, calendar and LinkedIn. Each person gets a strength score that rises and falls with real interaction, and you get flags on important relationships that are cooling.

Learning
98. Gap detection. The agent notices concepts you keep looking up, and terms in your meetings you’ve never looked into. It queues a 10-minute primer on each.
99. Lessons from your own work. The agent reviews your meeting transcripts and turns them into a curriculum, like “what you learned from the last 20 customer calls,” with the key patterns and quotes.
100. Steelman feed. Every week, the agent finds the strongest argument against each position you posted publicly, with sources.

Home and real estate
101. Off-market alerts. The agent watches public records for probate filings, expired listings and owners who’ve held 20+ years in your target neighborhoods. It drafts outreach to each owner.
102. Maintenance from model numbers. You give the agent your appliance and car model numbers once. It builds a maintenance schedule from the manuals, checks for recalls, and orders filters and parts when they’re due.
103. Apartment hunting on a schedule. The agent checks Facebook Marketplace every two hours, and sweeps Craigslist, SpareRoom and other sites at 8am and 8pm. It screens out scams and emails the landlord the minute a good listing appears.

What "not possible" examples am I missing??
